en.title: Dead Letter Queue
en.short: A message that will not process after several attempts is set aside — and a dead letter queue nobody watches is a rubbish bin.
en.body:
A queue that was empty yesterday has forty thousand messages today and none of them is being processed. The consumer is up, logging, and busy. Queue depth climbs.

And at the head of the queue sits one message whose amount field is a string rather than a number. The consumer takes it, errors, does not acknowledge, and the at-least-once delivery entry explained what happens next: the broker sends that same message again. Forever.

And this is a poison message, which gets no separate entry because it has no solution of its own — there is only a way of setting it aside.

The important thing is that the problem is not that one message. The problem is that this one message has stopped the thirty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine healthy messages behind it. One malformed row in a database spoils only itself; one malformed message at the head of a queue closes the whole flow.

A dead letter queue is a separate queue to which messages that have not processed after a set number of attempts are moved, so that the main queue can move on.

Its mechanism is a counter. Every delivery raises the message's attempt count by one. When it reaches the ceiling, instead of going back to the main queue the message goes to the dead letter queue. The first diagram draws that branch: the ordinary solid path, and the dashed path that opens at the ceiling.

In the example section, one poison message and three healthy ones share a queue. After three attempts the poison message is set aside and all three healthy messages have been processed — and their processing did not wait for those three attempts to finish, because a failed message returns to the tail of the queue rather than its head.

And that small detail matters more than the ceiling itself.

If a failed message goes straight back to the head, nothing else is processed until its attempts are exhausted. Returning it to the tail keeps the work flowing while that message still gets its attempts. In brokers' configuration that difference is usually one small option, and in the system's behaviour it is a large one.

And now the point that completes this pattern and is left out more than any other part of it.

A dead letter queue is not where a problem gets solved; it is where a problem is held until someone solves it. If that someone does not exist, the dead letter queue is a rubbish bin nobody ever opens.

And there is a distinction here worth stating plainly: every message in a dead letter queue is work not done, not a log line. An order that was not placed, a payment that was not refunded, an email that did not go. If there are five hundred messages in there, there are five hundred users for whom the thing they asked for did not happen.

So an alert on this queue's depth is part of the pattern and not an extra chore. A dead letter queue with no alarm is a half-implemented pattern — and the implemented half is precisely the part that looks good.

And what to do after the alarm, since not every message wants the same action.

The second diagram sets four common reasons beside their actions, and its point is that only the middle two are solved by replay. A malformed message replayed a thousand times comes right back; that one needs a fix in the producer. And a message that genuinely violated a rule — an order that can no longer be cancelled — is not a bug at all; it wants a human decision.

And choosing the ceiling, where too high and too low are both bad.

A low ceiling means a slightly longer transient error sends healthy messages to the dead letter queue. A high ceiling means a poison message eats consumer capacity for a long time. The usual number is small — three to five — and the reason is that the exponential backoff entry is responsible for separating out long failures and this ceiling is not meant to take its place.

And what has to travel with a message when it is set aside.

The message alone is not enough for debugging. What is needed: the last error, the number of attempts, the times of the first and last attempt, and the trace identifier tying the message back to the original request. The asynchronous communication entry said that in this style errors appear elsewhere and at another time; the dead letter queue is exactly that "elsewhere", and without those four items a message sitting there is a riddle rather than a clue.

And a distinction whose absence makes a dead letter queue look useless.

Sometimes a dead letter queue fills with messages that had nothing wrong with them and merely arrived while a dependency was down. If those get mixed in one place with genuinely malformed ones, whoever looks cannot tell them apart and eventually stops looking. Separating by error class — for which the transient failure entry supplied the tool — is what keeps this queue usable.

And a practical point about the dead letter queue itself.

A dead letter queue is a queue too and has the same limits: bounded capacity, bounded retention, and the ability to fill up. If messages are purged from it after seven days and nobody looks within those seven days, the pattern has done something that differs from "dropping" only in appearance. The backpressure entry counted three possible answers and this pattern is the third — spill elsewhere — with exactly the price stated there: you now have a second place that has to be watched.

And replay, which is an operation rather than a button.

Replay means putting that same message back on the main queue. And because the idempotency entry showed that a consumer has to tolerate repeats, replaying a message that was in fact half-done is harmless too — provided that tolerance was actually built. If it was not, a bulk replay of five hundred messages can create a new problem larger than the first one.

And a last point: a dead letter queue needs an owner like any other queue. If, at a service handover meeting, nobody can say who looks at this queue and how often, that queue has been a rubbish bin since its first day.

The counter, the ceiling, and the return to the tail — the three decisions the whole pattern consists of:

func (q *Queue) Run(msgs []Message, handle func(Message) error) {
	pending := append([]Message(nil), msgs...)
	for len(pending) > 0 {
		m := pending[0]
		pending = pending[1:]
		m.Attempts++
		if err := handle(m); err == nil {
			q.Done = append(q.Done, m.ID)
			continue
		}
		if m.Attempts >= q.MaxAttempts {
			q.Dead = append(q.Dead, m)
			continue
		}
		pending = append(pending, m) // back to the tail, not the head
	}
}
